plan.strategy: Specialize the dominant shape family (contiguous full-extent last-axis scatter, which is all 9 timed workloads) into a div-free row/column-block kernel.
plan.code_changes: Added _scatter_add_lastdim_kernel (2D grid: row x column-block, offsets = row*ncols+col, 4 runtime args) and a host dispatch that takes it when dim == ndim-1 and inp/index/src are contiguous with identical full shapes; the generic 8-slot ND kernel remains the fallback.
plan.hypothesis: The 8-strip div/mod decomposition is the dominant per-element cost (candidate 7.5ns/element vs reference 0.81ns/element on 1024^2) and the 34-argument launch is a large share of the ~140us fixed cost on 128^2. A div-free, 4-argument kernel over the same atomic scatter should improve every timing case, with the largest relative gain on the 1024^2/2048^2 shapes.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes 8 sequential runtime-valued int32 div/mod steps and 30 scalar arguments per element-block, so per-element index arithmetic collapses to one multiply-add; the 128^2 cases should also lose launcher argument overhead.

conclusion.root_cause: Div-free specialized addressing confirmed as the dominant large-shape win, but the residual large-case gap is a per-element data-dependent atomic/store cost (~4.6ns/element) that is invariant to conflict density, BLOCK, num_warps and masking; the small-shape gap is the fixed ~0.07ms per-launch floor paid twice (copy + atomic).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expectation met in direction and roughly in size: geo_mean 0.1903 -> 0.2888 (+51.8%), min_speedup 0.106 -> 0.172. Large cases improved as predicted by removing index arithmetic: 2048^2 31.50ms -> 19.55ms (1.61x) and 1024^2 7.91ms -> 4.95ms (1.60x), which is close to the 1.65x implied by dropping 8 div/mod steps per element. The small 128^2 cases improved much less (0.267 -> 0.197ms, 1.36x) because they are dominated by fixed per-launch cost, not element cost. A bounded target probe then located the remaining gap precisely: a tiny copy kernel alone costs ~0.07ms (per-launch floor), the 2048^2 atomic kernel is 19.49ms while a non-atomic data-dependent store of the same volume is 13.56ms and an affine copy of the same volume is 0.10ms; conflict density is irrelevant (unique-index and single-index atomics are both 19.48ms) and num_warps/mask removal change nothing. So the residual 5.8x versus the reference (0.8ns/element) is the framework's scalarized handling of data-dependent addresses, not index arithmetic. An all-affine dense formulation was measured: 43.6ms at 2048^2 (worse) but 0.067ms at 128^2 (better than either two-launch variant, exact match to the reference).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Dispatch the measured-cheaper dense all-affine kernel for small widths (ncols >= 32 and rows*ncols^2 cheap under a fitted cost model), keeping the atomic last-dim kernel for wide rows. Target-side probes (bounded, verified against torch.scatter_add) show the dense single-launch kernel at 0.067ms vs 0.101ms atomic vs 0.187ms current on 128^2, and 43.6ms vs 19.5ms on 2048^2, so the dispatch must be shape-dependent.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Two bounded probes separated three hypotheses that looked identical in end-to-end numbers: conflict density (no effect), launch shape (no effect), and data-dependent addressing (the entire residual). Always measure an affine-address kernel of the same data volume to bound what is achievable before optimizing a scatter.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 generic ND atomic (0.190) -> round 2 div-free specialized last-dim kernel (0.289). Next: shape-dependent dispatch between an all-affine dense kernel (small widths, one launch) and the atomic kernel (wide rows). Large-shape atomics look framework-bound; the remaining structural option is a sort-based formulation, which is out of budget this batch.
